“I now examined the death’s-head closely. Its outer boundaries—the lines of the design lying nearest the margin of the vellum—were much clearer than the rest. Evidently the operation of the heat had been incomplete or uneven. I at once lit a fire, and exposed each part of the parchment to its glowing warmth. At first this merely deepened the pale outlines of the skull; but as I continued the experiment, a figure appeared in the corner of the scrap diagonally across from the death’s-head. I initially took this figure for a goat. Further examination, however, convinced me that a kid was intended.”

“Ha! ha!” I exclaimed. “Certainly I have no business laughing at you—a million and a half in money is far too grave a subject for merriment—but you cannot be going to supply a third link in your chain. You will discover no particular connexion between your pirates and a goat. Pirates, as you know, have no concern with goats; those belong to the agricultural interest.”

“But I have just told you that the figure did not represent a goat.”

“Well, then, a kid—very nearly the same thing.”

“Very nearly, but not entirely,” replied Legrand. “You have perhaps heard of a certain Captain Kidd. I immediately regarded the animal’s figure as a sort of punning or hieroglyphic signature. I call it a signature because its place on the vellum prompted that notion. The death’s-head in the diagonally opposite corner similarly resembled a stamp or seal. Yet I was greatly vexed by the lack of anything besides—of the substance of my supposed document—of a text to accompany my context.”

“I suppose you looked for a letter between the seal and the signature.”

“Something to that effect. In truth, I was possessed by an irresistible foreboding of some immense good fortune approaching. I can hardly explain why. Possibly it was, after all, more a wish than a settled conviction; but are you aware that Jupiter’s foolish remarks about the bug’s being solid gold made a singular impression upon my imagination? Then there was that succession of accidents and coincidences—so exceedingly extraordinary. Do you notice what a sheer accident it was that all these things happened on the single day in the whole year when it has been, or is likely to be, cold enough to need a fire? And without that fire, or without the dog’s interference at the exact instant when he arrived, I should never have discovered the death’s-head, and consequently should never have obtained the treasure.”

The little man’s body was far too broad for his height, giving his whole figure an absurd roundness. Naturally, his feet were completely out of sight, though something hard and suspiciously like horn occasionally poked through a tear in the bottom of the basket—or, more accurately, in the top of the hat. His hands were enormous. His hair was very gray and gathered into a pigtail at the back. His nose was astonishingly long, crooked, and red; his eyes were large, bright, and sharp. His chin and cheeks, though wrinkled with age, were broad, swollen, and doubled with flesh. Yet nowhere on his head could anyone discover the slightest sign of ears. This curious little gentleman wore a loose coat of sky-blue satin, with matching tight breeches secured at the knees by silver buckles. His waistcoat was made of some bright yellow fabric, and a white taffeta cap sat at a jaunty angle on his head. To finish his outfit, a blood-red silk handkerchief wrapped around his throat and fell elegantly onto his chest in a fanciful bow of truly extraordinary size.

As I have already said, he had descended to about a hundred feet above the ground when the little old gentleman suddenly grew frightened and seemed unwilling to come any closer to earth. He therefore threw out some sand from a canvas bag, which he lifted with great difficulty, and his descent stopped instantly. Then, in a hurry and visibly upset, he pulled a large leather pocketbook from a side pocket of his coat. He balanced it suspiciously in his hand, stared at it in extreme surprise, and seemed quite astonished by its weight. At last he opened it and took out an enormous letter, sealed with red wax and carefully tied with red tape. He dropped it exactly at the feet of the mayor, Superbus Von Underduk. His Excellency bent down to pick it up. But the balloonist, still thoroughly unsettled and apparently having no further business to keep him in Rotterdam, now began busily preparing to leave. To rise again he needed to throw out some weight. He tossed out half a dozen bags, one after another, without bothering to empty them first. Most unfortunately, every single bag landed on the mayor’s back, sending him rolling over and over no fewer than twenty-one times before the eyes of every man in Rotterdam. It must not be imagined, however, that the great Underduk allowed such disrespect from the little old man to go unpunished.

“What is it?”

“Ten o’clock, sir.”

“What do you mean? Ten at night?”

“Yes, sir. You asked me to wake you.”

“Oh! I remember. All right, all right.”

After several sluggish attempts to fall asleep again, which the man expertly defeated by stirring the fire without pause for five minutes, he rose, threw on his hat, and went out. He entered the Temple and, after reviving himself by walking twice along the pavements of King’s Bench Walk and Paper Buildings, made his way to Stryver’s chambers.

Stryver’s clerk, who never took part in these conferences, had gone home, and Stryver himself opened the door. He wore slippers and a loose dressing gown, with his throat uncovered for comfort. Around his eyes he had that rather wild, strained, scorched look observable in all heavy drinkers of his class, from the portrait of Jeffries onward, and traceable beneath the various disguises of art in portraits from every age of drinking.

“You’re a little late, Memory,” said Stryver.

“About the usual time; perhaps fifteen minutes later.”

They entered a dingy room lined with books and strewn with papers, where a fire blazed. A kettle steamed on the hob, and amid the wreckage of papers a table gleamed, amply supplied with wine, brandy, rum, sugar, and lemons.

“You’ve had your bottle, I see, Sydney.”

“Two tonight, I think. I’ve been dining with today’s client; or watching him dine—it comes to the same thing!”

“That was an excellent point you made about the identification, Sydney. How did you think of it? When did it occur to you?”

“I thought he was a rather handsome fellow, and that I might have been much the same sort of fellow if I’d had any luck.”

Mr. Stryver laughed until his prematurely developed paunch shook.

“You and your luck, Sydney! Get to work, get to work.”

With a thoroughly sullen air, the jackal loosened his clothes, went into the next room, and returned with a large jug of cold water, a basin, and one or two towels. He soaked the towels, partly wrung them out, and folded them over his head in a hideous arrangement. Then he sat at the table and said, “Now I’m ready!”

“There isn’t much to boil down tonight, Memory,” Mr. Stryver said cheerfully, looking through his papers.

“How much?”

“Only two sets.”

“Give me the worst first.”

“There they are, Sydney. Fire away!”

The lion then settled on his back on a sofa beside the drinks table, while the jackal sat across from him at his own proper table, covered with papers, with bottles and glasses within easy reach.
